canonical_topic: Statistical Modeling of Spreads vs. Asset Prices
definition: Spreads between two prices differ fundamentally from individual asset prices: they can be zero or negative, so the lognormal distribution and percent-return concepts typically used for asset prices don't apply. Spreads are more commonly modeled with a normal distribution, or by using the ratio of the two prices (which behaves more like a lognormal distribution, e.g., tends not to go negative).
core_idea: Because individual commodity prices are almost always positive and are well described by a lognormal distribution, but spreads frequently cross zero, spread option models require different distributional assumptions than single-asset option models.
key_points: Asset prices are typically modeled as never going below zero but able to rise a lot (lognormal-like); this doesn't fit spreads.
Percent return is undefined for a spread that starts at zero, since that produces a division-by-zero error.
Spreads are commonly modeled with a normal distribution rather than lognormal.
An alternative approach models the ratio of the two prices instead of the difference, since the ratio behaves more like a lognormal distribution (e.g., stays non-negative).
relationships: Distinguishes spread modeling from standard single-asset lognormal option pricing (contrast with vanilla option assumptions).
caveats: Assuming a spread can be modeled the same way as a single commodity price (lognormal, never negative) is incorrect — spreads can be zero or negative.
